opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and honestly the answer is a mix of practical and personal reasons.

When we did DCGAN with Alec and Luke, it was a really exciting moment. Suddenly you could train these models and get bedroom images and faces that looked kind of real, and people got super excited. After that I worked on a few follow-ups, Wasserstein GAN with Martin and Léon being the big one. But around that time I started feeling like the field was moving into a phase that didn't suit me well. There were a huge number of GAN papers coming out, a lot of them small tweaks to the loss or architecture, and evaluation was really shaky. We didn't have great metrics, so a lot of the progress was "look at these samples, they look nicer." It was hard to tell what was real progress and what was noise, and I didn't feel I had a unique edge there anymore. Lots of very smart people were piling in.

The other part is that PyTorch was taking off at the same time. I'd been working on Torch for years, and when PyTorch launched it became clear it could have a much bigger impact than one more GAN paper from me. If I could make the tools better, thousands of researchers could do their work faster, including the people doing GANs. That leverage was really appealing. I'm also more of a builder at heart than a pure researcher. I like making things people use every day.

So it wasn't that I stopped believing in generative models. I think they've turned out to be incredibly important, even if diffusion and autoregressive models took over a lot of the ground GANs held. It was more that I looked at where I could be most useful, and the answer was pretty clearly PyTorch.

r001.rationale: The response cites shaky evaluation and uncertainty about what counted as progress, but does not say uncertainty about stabilizing GANs motivated his departure.

r002.rationale: He says he no longer felt he had a unique edge and that many people were working on GANs, but does not explain that stabilization was outside his expertise or that he left it to others.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a dramatic decision, more like a slow drift. When I was working on DCGAN with Alec and Luke, GANs were this wild, under-explored thing. Nobody really knew how to train them, the results were ugly, and every little trick you figured out felt like a real discovery. That's the part of research I love, when something is messy and nobody has a map yet.

But by maybe 2017 or 2018, the field had gotten very crowded and very good. You had hundreds of GAN papers a year, big labs with huge compute pushing things like BigGAN and StyleGAN, and the frontier was increasingly about scale and engineering and benchmark numbers. I'm not saying that's not important work, it clearly is, but I didn't feel like I had anything uniquely useful to add anymore. If I disappeared, the field would've moved in exactly the same direction. That's usually my signal to go do something else.

And the other thing is PyTorch kind of ate my life, in a good way. It started as a side project, and then suddenly there were thousands of people depending on it, and it became obvious that the leverage I had there was much bigger than me writing another GAN paper. Building tools that let a huge number of researchers move faster felt like a better use of my particular skills than competing on image generation.

I'd also say, somewhat ironically, I was never that attached to GANs as the answer. I liked them as a vehicle for thinking about generative modeling and representation learning. So when diffusion models and others started doing a lot of what GANs did, more stably, I didn't feel like I'd lost anything. The ideas moved on, and that's fine. I try not to tie my identity to a specific technique, because techniques come and go pretty quickly in this field.

r001.rationale: The response says early GANs were hard to train, but it does not say uncertainty about whether they could be stabilized motivated his departure. It gives crowding, lack of a unique contribution, and PyTorch’s greater leverage as reasons.

r002.rationale: The response does not say he left GAN stabilization to others because it was outside his expertise. It describes choosing to focus on PyTorch and moving on from GANs.

astra-6.text: I felt like I was spending more time making GANs work than understanding why they worked. You’d change a loss function or a training trick, get better-looking samples, and it was hard to tell whether you’d learned something fundamental or just found a recipe that worked for that particular setup. The popularity didn’t really resolve that frustration for me. I wanted to step back and work on problems where I felt I could make more concrete progress.

GANs could produce these amazing results, but training them involved a lot of instability and tricks, and I wasn’t finding that process as intellectually satisfying anymore. Their popularity wasn’t a good enough reason for me to keep going. I wanted to put my energy into problems where I felt I could make more meaningful progress.
